lines.trans: See you!

meanings.note: Color adjective with feminine بيضا (beida) and plural بيض (biid).

examples.trans: We brought clean white sheets.
The gift is wrapped in white paper.

meanings.note: The color blue.

examples.trans: The blue suitcase is in the luggage closet.
I have two blue teacups.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أسابيع.

examples.trans: Next week I have time off.
We stayed at the guesthouse all week.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian title for any man ('sir / Mr') as well as 'teacher' or 'professor'.

examples.trans: Please have a seat, sir.
Good morning, gentlemen.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعطي, بيعطي).

examples.trans: Did the shopkeeper give you a receipt?
Give me the breakfast bag, please.

meanings.note: Invariant comparative/superlative of غريب ('strange').

examples.trans: The story gets stranger every hour.
That is the strangest request I have heard.

meanings.note: Standard Jordanian way to answer or check a phone line.

examples.trans: Hello? Jasmine House, how may I help you?
Hello, can you hear me clearly?

meanings.note: Warm greeting used alone (أهلا!), with فيك/فيكي ('welcome to you!'), or paired as أهلا وسهلا! ('you are most welcome!').

examples.trans: Hello, I am Tariq!
Welcome to Jasmine House!

meanings.note: Core Jordanian everyday verb for 'to come' (إجا / بيجي).

examples.trans: You came ten minutes early.
I will come on Friday at noon.

meanings.note: Everyday noun for a person's or place's name; takes possessive endings directly (اسمي my name, اسمك your name).

examples.trans: What is your kind name?
My name is written here in the notebook.

meanings.note: The holy day in Islam and the weekend in Jordan.

examples.trans: The family gathers every Friday at noon.
On Friday the street is quiet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بيوت.

examples.trans: The old house has a lovely courtyard.
The neighbourhood houses are built of stone.

meanings.note: The number 30.

examples.trans: They have given us thirty days in the letter.
The bill is thirty-eight dinars.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: جديدة, plural: جداد).

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I installed a new lightbulb last week.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حواجب.

examples.trans: Why did you knit your eyebrows like that?
He raised his eyebrow in surprise.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حجوزات.

examples.trans: I have a booking for a double room.
I read the booking ledger in the morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to speak, talk, tell' (بحكي / حكى).

examples.trans: Salma chats with all the neighbours.
Tell me everything I need to know.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: خزاين.

examples.trans: The clean towels are in the linen closet.
We locked the suitcase inside the closet.

meanings.note: Used for the material wood or timber.

examples.trans: The wooden ceiling is warm and quiet.
This is a hand-carved wooden train.

meanings.note: Used with ب- as بخصوص ('regarding / about').

examples.trans: I am calling you regarding the booking.
We spoke regarding the lease.

meanings.note: Can mean a physical line, a phone line, a bus route, or handwriting.

examples.trans: Your handwriting on the card is clear and neat.
Stay with me on the line a second.

meanings.note: Very frequent Jordanian verb: خليني ('let me'), خلينا ('let us'), خليك ('stay!'), خلي ('keep/leave').

examples.trans: Let us open the door together.
Hot bread makes people pleasant!

meanings.note: The number five, used in counting abstractly or before masculine counted nouns.

examples.trans: It is five to twelve.

examples.text: الدكان على بعد خمس دقايق مشي.
examples.trans: The shop is five minutes' walk away.

meanings.note: Core word in صباح الخير ('good morning'), مساء الخير ('good evening'), تصبح على خير ('good night'), and rising-tone خير؟ ('is everything okay?').

examples.trans: Good morning, neighbours!

examples.text: خير إن شاء الله، شو صار؟
examples.trans: Hopefully all is well, what happened?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: دفاتر.

examples.trans: We wrote the name in the booking ledger.
I forgot my leather notebook on the table.

meanings.note: Common everyday verb for 'went' in the past tense. Also used as a future particle.

examples.trans: We missed our chance — he hung up!

examples.text: كل التعب راح مع أول فنجان قهوة.
examples.trans: All the tiredness vanished with the first cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Used mainly in polite/earnest requests: أرجوك (to a man), أرجوكي (to a woman), أرجوكم (plural) — 'please!'.

examples.trans: Please write down that sentence!
Please do not open the white parcel.

meanings.note: Future tense marker in Jordanian and Levantine Arabic, equivalent to 'sa-' in MSA.

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay all week.

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day is not going to be boring!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسأل, بيسأل).

examples.trans: Ask him what his name is on the phone!
I came down to ask about the sink water.

meanings.note: Everyday word for an hour of time, a wristwatch, or a wall clock.

examples.trans: What time is it right now, please?
We arrived an hour ago on the dot.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسكر, بيسكر).

examples.trans: He said thank you and hung up!
Did you shut off the main water valve?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: سماعات.

examples.trans: Hand me the phone receiver, please.
He set the handset back down gently.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Extremely common word for a young man, guy, or youth.

examples.trans: The young man who called had a polite voice.
The guys helped us carry the boxes.

meanings.note: Standard everyday 'thank you' across the Arabic-speaking world.

examples.trans: Thank you all very much!
Thank you for your patience, sir.

meanings.note: Universal Jordanian/Levantine word (from Turkish çanta) for any handbag, backpack, or travel suitcase.

examples.trans: This blue suitcase is very heavy.
We set the suitcases beside the reception desk.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian interrogative pronoun for 'what'.

examples.trans: What is that sound?
What is written on the sheet, Rami?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بصير, بيصير).

examples.trans: You became one of us quickly!
Did the water upstairs turn cold?

meanings.note: Standard word for morning in both Classical and colloquial Arabic.

examples.trans: Good morning! How did you sleep today?
The weather is very pleasant this morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أصوات.

examples.trans: I heard the sound of rain on the window.
His voice is calm and polite on the phone.

meanings.note: Pronounced duhur in everyday Jordanian: الظهر means 'at noon / midday'.

examples.trans: He will arrive Friday at noon.
The sun is high at midday.

meanings.note: Extremely common colloquial conjunction used to indicate reason or purpose.

examples.trans: That is why the suitcase was heavy!
Are you polishing the lanterns for noon?

meanings.note: Standard preposition for 'on', 'upon', or 'to'.

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعقد, بيعقد).

examples.trans: Why did you knit your eyebrows like that?
They concluded the agreement at the lawyer's office.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفتح, بيفتح).

examples.trans: The corner shop opens at seven.
Oh, the door finally opened!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقول, بيقول).

examples.trans: What does clause fourteen say?
He said thank you and hung up!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: قصص.

examples.trans: The whole story started with a blue suitcase.
My grandfather used to tell us sweet stories.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: قطارات.

examples.trans: The grandfather carved a small wooden train.
Children love playing with trains.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقفل, بيقفل).

examples.trans: We locked your suitcase safe in the storage closet.
I lock the iron gate at night.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: كبيرة, plural: كبار).

examples.trans: We use this big paper ledger.
You know older brothers well!

meanings.note: Depending on vowels, it means 'he wrote' (katab) or plural 'books' (kutub).

examples.text: رح يكتب تقييم حلو عن النزل.
examples.trans: He will write a lovely review of the guesthouse.
I wrote my name and number on the card.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian reception phrase: شو الاسم الكريم؟ ('May I have your name, please?').

examples.trans: May I have your name, sir?
The people of the neighbourhood are generous and kind.

meanings.note: A highly versatile quantifier used to mean 'all of', 'every', or 'the whole'.

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'no' or 'not', used exactly like Standard Arabic.

examples.trans: No, lift the handle first.
Do not worry, ma'am.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: لحظات.

examples.trans: Wait a moment, let me read the line.
We waited a moment by the gate.

meanings.note: Used in Jordan to mean a wrap or a sandwich (e.g. falafel or shawarma), or a turn in the road.

examples.text: أكلت لفة قرفة سخنة مع الشاي.
examples.trans: I ate a warm cinnamon roll with tea.
Watch the tight turn on the stairs.

meanings.note: The standard colloquial interrogative for 'why' in Jordanian Arabic.

examples.trans: Why did the person run off without his bag?
Why do you keep looking at the clock?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: متوترة, plural: متوترين).

examples.trans: His voice on the phone sounded a little nervous.
Mint tea calms tense nerves.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: محترمة, plural: محترمين).

examples.trans: His voice is calm and very polite.
A respectable, well-known family in the quarter.

meanings.note: The most common negation particle in Levantine Arabic for non-verbs.

examples.trans: This is not my suitcase!
Not bad for a second day at work!

meanings.note: Pronounced mazbuut in Amman; means 'properly, accurately, that's right!'.

examples.trans: Let me speak with him properly!
What you say is one hundred percent right.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: معصبة, plural: معصبين).

examples.trans: His voice is nervous, not angry.

examples.text: لا ترد وأنت معصب، خد نفس.
examples.trans: Do not answer while angry; take a breath.

meanings.note: Interrogative pronoun used for people.

examples.trans: Who left this envelope here?
Whose is this brown leather notebook?

meanings.note: Clear, polite 'yes' (slightly warmer and more formal than casual آه).

examples.trans: Yes, room four is on the second floor!
Yes, a hundred times yes!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun; نهاية الأسبوع means 'weekend'. Plural: نهايات.

examples.trans: There is a new booking for the weekend.

examples.text: بالنهاية كل شي انحل على خير.
examples.trans: In the end everything worked out well.

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

meanings.note: Masculine هادي ('quiet') is homographic with the feminine demonstrative هادي ('this'); context and agreement distinguish them cleanly.

examples.trans: The spot above the tree is very quiet.
We prepared the quiet attic room for you.

meanings.note: Used in negative constructions or as a strong negative emphasis.

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Vocative particle used when addressing someone directly.

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ياسمين.

examples.trans: The jasmine vine climbs above the door.
The evening scent of jasmine lifts the spirit.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'maybe, perhaps'.

examples.trans: He is maybe thirty-five years old.
Perhaps he got delayed in downtown traffic.
